edits.after: The following was the COMP 536 Project 1 contract. It is retained as a worked example, not a COMP 521 grading requirement:

edits.before: Prove otherwise with validation, not hope.
edits.after: Support correctness claims with tests and validation evidence.
Every plot is a diagnostic; validation also needs a stated reference or expectation.

edits.before: **Assume your code is wrong until proven otherwise.**
edits.after: **Support correctness claims with tests and validation evidence.**

edits.before: Then prove yourself wrong by finding evidence of correctness.
edits.after: Then test that assumption with independent evidence.

edits.before: This is $O(\log n)$ instead of $O(n)$ — much faster for long code paths.
edits.after: With ordered checkpoints and a failure that can be localized to one half, checkpoint decisions grow as $O(\log n)$. Arbitrary bugs do not automatically satisfy that assumption.

edits.before: A passing test suite means: "All requirements I wrote down are satisfied."
edits.after: A passing test suite means the implemented checks passed for the tested cases; omitted requirements and untested cases remain open.

edits.before: Git remembers everything. Commit first, then delete.
edits.after: Git preserves committed content. Uncommitted and ignored files need separate protection.

git status
git diff
git add path/to/changed_file.py

git log --oneline -- filename.py
git diff <baseline-commit> -- filename.py
# After inspecting the change:
git restore --source=<baseline-commit> -- filename.py

edits.before: Nothing is ever truly lost if it's in git.
edits.after: Choose the saved baseline commit explicitly. Restoring replaces current uncommitted contents; a commit does not protect untracked or ignored files.

edits.before: If you deeply understand the problem, the code writes itself. If you don't, no amount of debugging will save you.
edits.after: Understanding the problem gives you a contract and predictions to test. Implementation still requires careful work. When repeated patches fail, revisit the assumptions and the smallest case you can explain by hand.
